title: Applying for a PhD Without Publications: Show Your Research Preparation
seoTitle: PhD Without Publications: Show Your Research Preparation
seoDescription: Apply for a PhD without publications by explaining research decisions, your project contribution and accurately labelled reports or other outputs.
intro: A publication can support an application, but requirements depend on the project and programme. Show how you have developed research skills through a dissertation, technical work, reading or another relevant project.
description:
Check whether a publication is actually required

Read the project and programme criteria before deciding that you are ineligible. A publication can support an application, but its importance depends on the field and selection process. If the advert explicitly requires a particular research output or experience, address that requirement honestly. If it does not, focus on the preparation you can demonstrate.

A lack of publications and a lack of research experience are different issues. You may have completed a dissertation, developed a method, collected data or worked on a technical investigation without producing a paper. Explain that work clearly and let the reader assess its relevance.

Make your contribution visible

Describe the scientific or technical question, the approach and your own tasks. If the work was collaborative, distinguish your contribution from the group’s results. Discuss a methodological choice and a limitation. These details help the reader understand how you think about research rather than simply what topic appeared in your degree.

Where you are allowed to share material, include an accessible report, code repository, poster or other suitable output. Check ownership, confidentiality and any restrictions before making data or documents public. A broken or undocumented repository does not help a reader understand the work.

Use references and the proposal carefully

A referee who supervised relevant work can provide specific evidence about your preparation. Supply accurate reminders of the project and the application instructions. Do not ask a referee to endorse achievements they have not observed.

If a proposal is requested, connect the question to the destination group and describe a feasible plan. If the position advertises a fixed project, show your understanding of that project instead of submitting an unrelated proposal. A thoughtful application should identify what you know and what training you would need.

Label research outputs accurately

Keep published papers, accepted work, submitted manuscripts and work in progress in clearly labelled categories. A preprint is not automatically a peer-reviewed publication. Do not create an empty publication section just to make a CV resemble a senior researcher’s.

Avoid rushing a weak manuscript into a venue solely to obtain a publication line. Choose an output because it communicates useful work and meets the standards appropriate to your field. For an application, accuracy matters more than inflating the number of items listed.

Prepare a project summary

Write a short summary that answers five questions: what was the problem, what did you do, why that method, what did the results show, and what remains uncertain? Use it to prepare the CV, statement and interview. The wording should change for the document, but the underlying facts should stay consistent.

Package one piece of research well

Choose a dissertation or project you can discuss in detail. Prepare a short summary covering the question, your method, your contribution, the findings and a limitation. If you have code or data you are permitted to share, provide a tidy repository or supporting file. A publication is a separate outcome; do not relabel coursework as a paper or describe an unfinished manuscript as accepted. The application should help the reader assess research preparation using the evidence you do have rather than apologise repeatedly for the evidence you do not.

Show the process behind the output

A research paper is one possible output of preparation, not the only way to explain it. If the programme does not require publications, use a dissertation, project or research role to show how you work. Describe the question, relevant literature, method, your contribution and what the evidence did or did not support.

The most useful detail is often a decision. Explain why you chose a baseline, changed a measurement procedure or rejected an interpretation. That gives the reader something more concrete than saying you have strong analytical skills. Keep the scale of the claim proportionate to what you actually did.

Choose an honest output label

MaterialAccurate description
Degree dissertationA thesis or dissertation submitted for the named qualification.
Public technical reportA report with its actual venue and review status stated.
PreprintA public manuscript, distinguished from peer-reviewed publication.
Submitted manuscriptA paper under consideration, without implying acceptance.
Work in progressAn incomplete draft or project with proposed work clearly separated.

Do not submit to an unsuitable journal simply to create a publication line before an application deadline. Assess the venue, review process, costs and relevance independently. A rushed or misleading output can be harder to defend than a clear account of substantial unpublished work.

Prepare a two-minute research explanation

Use one sentence for the problem, a few for the methods and your role, and a final sentence for the main limitation or next question. Practise explaining it without slides. If the project was collaborative, identify your contribution before discussing the team's broader result.

References can help establish how independently you worked and how you responded to difficulty. Choose people who observed those behaviours and give them factual reminders. Do not ask them to endorse a publication status or research result that is not accurate.

Should I leave the publications section empty?

You can omit an irrelevant empty section unless the template asks for it. Use the space for research projects, skills and outputs that you can describe honestly.

Does no publication mean no chance of a funded PhD?

There is no reliable universal probability. Read the vacancy's requirements and assess your preparation against the project. Eligibility and research fit are more useful questions than an unsupported success-rate estimate.

Share material you are allowed to share

If a thesis or project uses confidential data, do not publish it merely to strengthen an application. Ask whether a redacted report, abstract or private submission is permitted. Explain access restrictions accurately and identify what you can discuss. A credible account of your contribution does not require exposing material owned by an employer or collaborator.

Official sources and further reading

Requirements and policies should be checked for your programme and application date. Sources checked on 19 October 2026.

  • Oxford: graduate application requirements
  • Cambridge: postgraduate entry requirements

Related guides

  • How to Email a PhD Supervisor: 7 Templates and Practical Tips
  • Academic CV for PhD Applications: Structure and an Example
  • PhD Research Proposal for Europe: Structure and a Worked Example
